questions.question: The Chinese Pilgrim ‘Xuan Zang’ lived in the court of which King ?
questions.questionHtml: The Chinese Pilgrim ‘Xuan Zang’ lived in the court of which King ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: 'C) Harsha.'

Key Points

  • Xuan Zang lived in the court of King Harsha.
    • Xuan Zang, also known as Hiuen Tsang, was a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim and scholar who visited India during the 7th century CE.
    • He resided at the court of Harsha, the ruler of the Vardhana dynasty, who ruled over northern India during this period.
    • Harsha was a great patron of Buddhism, and his court welcomed scholars and pilgrims, which provided Xuan Zang the opportunity to study and document Indian culture, religion, and society.
    • Xuan Zang’s detailed accounts are recorded in his work, "Si-Yu-Ki" (Records of the Western World), which provides valuable insights into 7th-century India.

Incorrect Statements

  • Chandragupta
    • Chandragupta Maurya was the founder of the Mauryan Empire in the 4th century BCE, much earlier than Xuan Zang’s time.
  • Samudragupta
    • Samudragupta, a ruler of the Gupta dynasty, reigned in the 4th century CE, earlier than Xuan Zang’s visit to India.
  • Kanishka
    • Kanishka, a ruler of the Kushan Empire, lived during the 1st–2nd century CE, long before Xuan Zang’s time.
    • Although Kanishka was a great patron of Buddhism, Xuan Zang did not visit his court.

Hence, the correct option is: C) Harsha.

Additional Information

  • Xuan Zang’s Contributions:
    • He studied at Nalanda University, one of the greatest centers of learning in ancient India, during his stay in India.
    • His accounts describe the prosperity, governance, and religious practices of Harsha’s kingdom.
  • Harsha’s Religious Policies:
    • Although initially a follower of Hinduism, Harsha became a patron of Buddhism later in his life.
    • He organized Buddhist assemblies and built stupas to promote the teachings of the Buddha.

questions.question: In the three-tier structure of the Panchayati Raj system in India, which body is elected at the grassroots level?
questions.questionHtml: In the three-tier structure of the Panchayati Raj system in India, which body is elected at the grassroots level?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Gram Panchayat.

Key Points

  • The Gram Panchayat is the grassroots-level body in the three-tier Panchayati Raj system in India.
  • It is directly elected by the people of the village, forming the first tier of the Panchayati Raj system.
  • The Gram Panchayat is responsible for local governance and development activities in villages.
  • Its members are elected for a term of five years by the eligible voters in the village.
  • The head of the Gram Panchayat is called the Sarpanch, who is also elected by the villagers.

Additional Information

  • Panchayati Raj System in India:
    • The Panchayati Raj system is a decentralized form of governance in which gram panchayats are the basic units of administration.
    • It was constitutionalized through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
    • The system has three levels: Gram Panchayat (village level), Panchayat Samiti (block level), and Zila Parishad (district level).
  • Roles and Responsibilities of Gram Panchayat:
    • Implementation of development programs such as rural housing, sanitation, and drinking water supply.
    • Maintenance of public assets like roads, schools, and community centers.
    • Promotion of literacy, health, and awareness programs in rural areas.
  • Funding of Gram Panchayats:
    • Funds are provided through grants from the central and state governments, revenue generated locally, and other sources.
    • The Finance Commission recommends financial allocations to Panchayati Raj institutions.
  • Importance of Grassroots Governance:
    • It ensures that governance is inclusive and caters to the specific needs of rural populations.
    • It encourages local participation in decision-making and promotes accountability.

questions.question: Which of the following indicates the system introduced by Lord Cornwallis granting legal ownership of land to the zamindars in Bengal in order to get a fixed revenue by a fixed date?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following indicates the system introduced by Lord Cornwallis granting legal ownership of land to the zamindars in Bengal in order to get a fixed revenue by a fixed date?
questions.solution: The Permanent Settlement was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793, granting legal ownership of land to the zamindars in Bengal. This system aimed to secure a fixed revenue for the British East India Company by ensuring zamindars paid a fixed amount by a specified date. In contrast, the Ryotwari System was implemented mainly in Madras, Bombay, and parts of Assam, focusing on direct settlement between the government & individual cultivators. The Mahalwari System applied to the North-Western Provinces, central India, and Punjab, involving revenue settlement with village communities rather than individual landowners. The Taluqdari System was a form of land tenure in North India, emphasizing landlords as intermediaries between the cultivators & the government, but it was not specifically designed for revenue collection as the Permanent Settlement was.

questions.question: Who among the following Mauryan king fasted to death and died at Shravanabelagola?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following Mauryan king fasted to death and died at Shravanabelagola?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is Chandragupta Maurya.

Key Points

  • Chandragupta lived as an ascetic at Shravanabelagola for several years before fasting to death as per the practice of sallekhana, according to the Digambara legend.
  • Chandragupta was the founder of the Mauryan dynasty (reigned c. 321–c. 297 BCE) and the first emperor to unify most of India under one administration.
  • He is credited with saving the country from maladministration and freeing it from foreign domination.

Additional Information

Bindusara - 

  • Bindusara, also known as Bindusara Maurya, was the 2nd Mauryan emperor, who seized the throne in 297 BCE.
  • He was a Greek Amitrochates (b.c 320 BCE—died 272/3 BCE).
  • According to Greek historians, he was known as Amitrochates, which is derived from the Sanskrit word amitraghata, which means “destroyer of opponents.”

Dasharatha - 

  • Dasaratha Maurya, grandson of Ashoka the Great, ruled as the fourth emperor of the Mauryan Empire from 232 BCE to 224 BCE. Here's a detailed breakdown of his reign:
  • Background:
    • Ascended the throne after his grandfather, Ashoka.
    • Unlike Ashoka, who was known for his military conquests before embracing Buddhism, Dasaratha's reign is associated with the decline of the Mauryan Empire.
  • Challenges during his reign:
    • Loss of Territories: Several regions of the vast Mauryan Empire declared independence during Dasaratha's rule. This weakened the empire's central authority.
    • Limited Ability: Historians believe Dasaratha may not have possessed the strong leadership qualities needed to hold the empire together.
  • Positive aspects:
    • Continued Ashoka's Policies: Dasaratha is known for upholding the social and religious policies established by his grandfather, particularly the promotion of Dharma (righteousness) and non-violence.
    • Patronage of Ajivikas: Inscriptions in the Barabar Caves suggest Dasaratha may have patronized the Ajivika sect, a non-vedic philosophical tradition that existed alongside Buddhism during that period.
  • Legacy:
    • Dasaratha's reign is considered a turning point in Mauryan history. The decline of the empire that began under him continued in the following years.
    • He was the last Mauryan emperor to leave behind epigraphical evidence (inscriptions) of his rule.
    • Dasaratha's successor was his cousin, Samprati, who attempted to revive the empire.
  • Ashoka - 
    • Ashoka the Great (r. 268-232 BCE) was the third king of the Mauryan Empire (322-185 BCE)
    • He is best known for his renunciation of war, development of the concept of dhamma (pious social conduct), and promotion of Buddhism as well as his effective reign of a nearly pan-Indian political entity.

questions.question: Milind Rege, the former cricket captain and selector who passed away at 76, represented which Indian state in domestic cricket?

questions.question: By which time Governor has to return an ordinary bill to the concerned State Legislature for reconsideration?
questions.questionHtml: By which time Governor has to return an ordinary bill to the concerned State Legislature for reconsideration?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option 3.

Key Points

  • The Constitution of India does not specify any time limit within which a Governor must return an ordinary bill to the State Legislature for reconsideration. Hence, option 3 is correct.
  • Governor’s Role in Bill Assent (Article 200):
    • When a State Legislature passes an ordinary bill, the Governor has the following options:
      • a) Give assent to the bill.
      • b) Withhold assent to the bill.
      • c) Return the bill for reconsideration to the State Legislature (except for Money Bills).
      • d) Reserve the bill for the President’s consideration.
  • No Time Frame:
    • The Constitution does not prescribe any specific time frame for the Governor to act on the bill.
    • This often leads to delays, as the Governor may sit on the bill indefinitely, causing controversies regarding the misuse of power.
  • Returning for Reconsideration:
    • If the Governor returns the bill for reconsideration, the State Legislature can:
      • Repass the bill with or without amendments.
      • If the bill is sent back to the Governor again, the Governor is bound to give assent to the bill.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an example of a stringed instrument?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is not an example of a stringed instrument?
questions.solution: The Dhol is a double-sided barrel drum primarily used as an accompanying instrument in regional music forms. It is not a stringed instrument but a percussion instrument played with two wooden sticks. In contrast, string instruments produce sound through vibrating strings and include instruments like the guitar, violin, and harp. The Dhol is specifically played using a stick known as the dagga for the bass side. This distinction makes the Dhol different from string instruments, which are characterized by their method of sound production via strings.

questions.question: Which court in India is responsible for handling civil cases like property disputes, divorce and consumer problems?
questions.questionHtml: Which court in India is responsible for handling civil cases like property disputes, divorce and consumer problems?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Civil Court.

Key Points

  • Civil Courts in India are responsible for handling disputes related to property, divorce, consumer problems, contracts, and other civil matters. These courts deal with non-criminal issues exclusively.
  • The jurisdiction of Civil Courts is governed under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which provides a detailed procedure for filing and resolving civil cases.
  • Civil Courts operate at different levels, including District Courts, which are the primary courts for civil litigation, and High Courts, which have appellate jurisdiction for civil cases.
  • These courts can issue orders such as injunctions, decrees, or compensation awards to resolve disputes between parties.
  • In matters of consumer disputes, the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions (District, State, and National Levels) also function as specialized quasi-judicial bodies under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

Additional Information

  • Revenue Court:
    • Revenue Courts deal primarily with matters related to land revenue, tenancy disputes, and agricultural land ownership.
    • These courts operate under the state-specific laws like the Land Revenue Code or Tenancy Acts.
    • They are not responsible for handling civil disputes like property disputes or divorce.
  • Criminal Court:
    • Criminal Courts handle cases related to offenses and crimes such as theft, assault, murder, and other violations of criminal law.
    • These courts operate under the Indian Penal Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
    • They have no jurisdiction over civil matters like property disputes or divorce.
  • Sessions Court:
    • Sessions Courts are part of the criminal court system and handle serious criminal cases like rape, murder, and kidnapping.
    • They are governed under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and have no jurisdiction over civil disputes.
  • Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
    • The Consumer Protection Act provides for the establishment of consumer courts to address grievances related to defective products, unfair trade practices, and service deficiencies.
    • These courts act as specialized quasi-judicial bodies and are distinct from Civil Courts.

Important Points

  • Hierarchy of Civil Courts:
    • Civil Courts in India are structured into a hierarchy: District Courts (lowest level), High Courts (state level), and the Supreme Court (national level).
    • District Courts primarily handle trials, while High Courts and the Supreme Court deal with appeals and constitutional matters.
  • Code of Civil Procedure, 1908:
    • This code provides the legal framework for filing and resolving civil disputes.
    • It includes provisions for jurisdiction, filing of suits, evidence collection, and execution of decrees.

questions.question: Which of the following part of India receives the first monsoon in summer?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following part of India receives the first monsoon in summer?
questions.solution: The Western Ghats receive their first monsoon in summer, which lasts from July to September. The south-west monsoon causes rainfall in most states of India. questions.question: The 16th Finance Commission (FC-16) has defined "Income Distance" based on which of the following calculations?
questions.questionHtml: The 16th Finance Commission (FC-16) has defined "Income Distance" based on which of the following calculations?

options.text: The difference between a state’s per capita GSDP and the state with the highest per capita GSDP.
options.html: The difference between a state’s per capita GSDP and the state with the highest per capita GSDP.

options.text: The difference between a state’s per capita GSDP and the average per capita GSDP of all states.
options.html: The difference between a state’s per capita GSDP and the average per capita GSDP of all states.

options.text: The difference between a state’s per capita GSDP and the national average GDP per capita.
options.html: The difference between a state’s per capita GSDP and the national average GDP per capita.

options.text: The difference between a state’s per capita GSDP and the average per capita GSDP of the top three large states with the highest per capita GSDP.
options.html: The difference between a state’s per capita GSDP and the average per capita GSDP of the top three large states with the highest per capita GSDP.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is The difference between a state’s per capita GSDP and the average per capita GSDP of the top three large states with the highest per capita GSDP.

In News

  • The 16th Finance Commission (FC-16) introduced a refined definition for 'Income Distance' to determine horizontal devolution for 2026-31.

Key Points

  • Income distance is now calculated as the gap between a state's per capita GSDP and the average of the top three large states with the highest per capita GSDP.
  • The Per capita GSDP is computed as the average over the period 2018-19 to 2023-24.
  • To ensure data accuracy and fairness, the pandemic year of 2020-21 has been excluded from this average calculation.
  • States with a lower per capita GSDP receive a higher share under this parameter to promote fiscal equity across the country.
  • Income Distance Statistics:
    • Weightage in FC-16 - 42.5%
    • Calculation Period - 2018-19 to 2023-24 (Excluding 2020-21)
    • Benchmark - Average of top 3 large states

Additional Information

  • GSDP (Gross State Domestic Product)
    • It represents the total value of all finished goods and services produced within a state's borders during a specific period.
  • Equity vs. Efficiency
    • Income Distance is an 'equity' parameter (helping poorer states), while the new 'Contribution to GDP' is an 'efficiency' parameter (rewarding productive states).
  • 15th FC Comparison
    • The 15th FC typically used the distance from the single highest-income state, whereas the 16th FC uses an average of the top three to create a more stable benchmark.
  • Horizontal Devolution
    • The allocation of the 41% tax pool among states based on the formula containing Income Distance, Population, Area, etc.

    • Other Initiatives: Three dedicated chemical parks will be set up to enhance domestic production and reduce import dependency. A scheme for container manufacturing was also proposed.

questions.question: In pea, a pure tall plant (TT) is crossed with a short plant (tt). What will be the ratio of pure tall plants to short plants in the F 2 generation ?
questions.questionHtml: In pea, a pure tall plant (TT) is crossed with a short plant (tt). What will be the ratio of pure tall plants to short plants in the F<sub>2</sub> generation ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1: 1.

Key Points

  • '​Pure' plants refer to the homozygous condition in plants and 'hybrid' refers to the heterozygous plants.
  • Homozygous - It is the condition in which the pair of alleles determining a phenotype is identical, either both dominant (TT) or both recessive (tt).
  • Heterozygous - It is the condition where 2 different types of alleles are present, one dominant and one recessive (Tt).
  • When a pure tall plant (TT) is crossed with a pure short plant (tt), the F1 generation produces heterozygous tall (Tt) plants.
  • Upon selfing the F1 generation, that is, crossing two heterozygous tall plants, the following numbers of the F2 generation are obtained phenotypically:
    • Three tall plants and one short plant
  • Whereas, genotypically, the following ratio is obtained:
    • One pure tall plant, two heterozygous tall plants, and one pure short plant.
  • Therefore, considering the genotype, the ratio of pure tall plants to pure short plants in the F2 generation is 1:1. Hence, Option 1 is correct.

Mistake Points

  • Please note here that the question asks about the ratio of "pure" tall plants to short plants in F2 generation.
  • The usual ratio of 3:1 is for "all" tall plants to short plants.
  • Pure Tall plants : Hybrid Tall plants : Short/Dwarf plants = TT : Tt : tt = 1:2:1
  • Therefore, Pure tall : Pure short = 1:1
